GEOLOGIC SETTING A
The Valley and Ridge Province of Pennsyl-
Appalachian
vania is composed of lithified sediments shed
Plateau
off the ancient Appalachian Mountains as they
formed in a series of orogenies spanning the
Late Ordovician to Early Permian. During the
Acadian orogeny, the Oatka Creek Member of
the Marcellus Formation was deposited as the Valley and
basinal shale equivalent of the Catskill Delta Ridge
complex under anoxic-sulfidic conditions Great Valley and
(Werne et al., 2002; Lash and Engelder, 2011, Piedmont
and references therein). Anoxic-sulfidic condi-
tions promote the formation and preservation of
iron-sulfide remanence carriers like pyrrhotite Devonian Pennsylvanian
(Fe S) and greigite (FeS) at the expense of
1–x 3 4 Silurian Mississippian
iron oxides like magnetite (FeO; Horng and
3 4
Roberts, 2006; Rowan et al., 2009). Radiometri- Ordovician Drill Site Loca(cid:31)on
cally calibrated biostratigraphy gives an age of
388–389 Ma for the Oatka Creek Member in
the northwest Appalachian foreland (Brett et al.,
2011; Kaufmann, 2006).
Deformation of the Appalachian foreland
took place during the Alleghany orogeny.
Stamatakos et al. (1996) demonstrated that
remagnetization of Appalachian basin rocks
occurred relatively quickly, in the latter part of
the Permian, compared to the propagation
of folds through the basin. Permian paleomag-
netic directions appear to postdate folding near
the hinterland margin, be synfolding in the cen-
tral part of the Valley and Ridge, and predate
folding toward the Appalachian Plateau. The
rocks collected for this study were recovered
from an area that closely neighbors rocks with
synfolding Permian magnetizations to the east
and prefolding Permian magnetizations to the
west (Fig. 1; fig. 5 in Stamatakos et al., 1996).
The bend in the Appalachians known as the
Pennsylvania salient predates the episode of
Permian remagnetization, as paleomagnetic
directions of Permian age are statistically indis-
tinguishable on the north and south limbs of lel to bedding observed in the surface outcrop to 110 mT). Measurements of remanence and
the salient (Stamatakos and Hirt, 1994). This (dip angle = 30°, and dip direction = 167°). AF demagnetization were performed using a

Figure 1. Location and drilling procedure: (A) The AX 50.8-mm-
diameter drill core was extracted near Sunbury, Pennsylvania, in
the Valley and Ridge Province. Bedrock geology is from Miles and
Whitfield (2001). (B–C) The core was cut in half along dip direction,
and 25 mm drill cores were removed in the laboratory. Subsamples
for drilling-induced remanence (DIR) experiments were obtained
by partitioning paleomagnetic specimens into interior and exterior
segments. Drilling location is 40.85° N, 76.74° W.

Thermal Demagnetization
Thermal demagnetization of specimens from
the upper 100 m of the core yielded two com-
ponents of magnetization. The first component
was isolated between 100 °C and 275 °C and
points west and intermediate to steeply down in
geographic coordinates. The second component
was isolated between temperatures of 300 °C
and up to 360 °C and points south and shal-
low in geographic coordinates (Fig. 2A). NRM

Figure 2. Thermal demagnetization results. (A–B) Typical vector endpoint diagrams
(Zjiderveld, 1967) of thermal demagnetization results in geographic coordinates from the
upper 100 m of the drill core (A) and the lower 20 m (B). Gray dashed arrows are placed
adjacent to demagnetization steps used to indicate the principal component analysis (PCA)
fits (Kirshvink 1980). The range of demagnetization steps (DEMAG), the direction of the paleo-
magnetic vector in geographic (GEO) and tilt-corrected (TILT) coordinates, and the maximum
angu lar deviation (MAD) for the fits are given. (C–D) Thermal decay of natural remanent
magnetization (NRM) for specimens shown in (A) and (B) respectively. Open squares in (D)
indicate demagnetization steps omitted from the vector endpoint diagram for clarity.

SEM and EDS
Basic petrographic observations of polished
thin sections revealed opaque, euhedral miner-
als crosscutting calcite-rich microfossils. SEM
observations showed that these grains are iron
sulfides, with elemental abundances similar to
pyrrhotite (Figs. 13A and 13B). Framboid struc-

6.0E–08
mens from the lower portion of the core were
completely demagnetized by 450 °C, with
4.0E–08
stability in the high-coercivity component up
to 260 °C and rapid decay until 320 °C. The
2.0E–08
lower-coercivity components gradually decayed
over this range, although the 45 mT component
0.0E+00 decayed little between 200 °C and 320 °C, and
then rapidly decayed. It is clear that the lower
portion of the core is dominated by iron sulfides,
with no remanence stable at high temperatures,
indicating an absence of magnetite. This behav-
ior is consistent with samples taken from the
horizon dominated by the component D direc-
tion (425–430 m) and the horizon below domi-
nated by component C directions (435–450 m).
We conclude that pyrrhotite is likely the high-
coercivity remanence carrier, as in the upper
part of the core. The lower-coercivity rema-
nence carrier could be greigite or a low-coerciv-
ity fraction of pyrrhotite.
Origins of Magnetic Components
Drilling-Induced Remanence
Regardless of clear changes in mineralogi-
cal composition between the upper and lower
portions of the drill core, the overwhelming
majority of samples from both sections yielded
a low-coercivity remanence with west and inter-
mediate to steep directions (component A; Figs.
3, 4, and 6). The direction and resistance to AF
treatment of component A are consistent with
drilling-induced remanences observed in basalt
drill cores from Audunsson and Levi (1989).
Those authors observed radially inward mag-
netic directions with stability to AF demagneti-
zation similar to a ~10 mT IRM, and decreas-
ing intensity toward the center of the drill core.
Our component A direction matches all of these
characteristics, except that the decay of the natu-
ral remanence is consistent with a stronger mag-
netic field of the drill string than that observed
in Audunsson and Levi’s core. Otherwise, the
component A direction points toward the cen-
ter of the core (in geographic coordinates, west
and steeply down for specimens taken from the
east portion of the core), and NRM intensity is
unequivocally higher in specimens closer to the
cutting surface (Fig. 8).
The relatively strong clustering of compo-
nent A in the exterior samples compared to
the directions removed over the same coerciv-
ity range from interior samples indicates that

However, the geographic direction of compo-
nent A is not parallel with a modern-day field
direction. It seems likely that if a modern-day
overprint existed, it was erased and replaced by
the magnetic field direction of the drill string.
None of the other components of magnetiza-
tion had modern-day field directions or curved
demagnetization paths that would suggest
higher-coercivity components are contaminated
by a modern-day direction.

remanence is reasonable given the temporal

1.2E–02 original orientation, and we corrected all the

8.0E–03 wise vertical-axis rotation.
The possibility that component B results
4.0E–03
from overlap between components A and C can
also be addressed by the stratigraphic pattern
0.0E+00
0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 of AF results (Fig. 14). Component B is only
observed in the upper 100 m of the core, where
2.0E–02 Lowrie tests and SEM observations yielded
evidence of detrital magnetite. Component B
1.6E–02
is not observed in the lower 20 m of the core,
1.2E–02 despite the persistence of components A and C,
and where Lowrie tests indicated only iron-sul-
8.0E–03
fide remanence carriers are present. Thus, the
4.0E–03 results show that simple overprinting of com-
ponent C with component A does not produce
0.0E+00
0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 component B, and that component B is only
observed where magnetite is present. Based
on these observations, we reject the hypothesis
that components A and C overlapped to produce
component B. Instead, we suggest that com-
ponent B is a detrital remanence in magnetite,
which is isolated from the drilling remanence
and the chemical remanence in pyrrhotite.
